Stump
stŭmp
n. (the base left after felling; rendering Hebrew iqqar)
Middle English stumpe. A stump is what remains when a tree is cut — in Scripture, sometimes a ruin and sometimes a reservation.

Biblical Definition

A stump is the base left after felling. Nebuchadnezzar's dream tree is cut down but the stump is preserved: “leave the stump of his roots in the earth, even with a band of iron and brass… till seven times pass over him” (Dan 4:15) — and the interpretation is that his kingdom shall be sure to him after he has known that the heavens do rule (Dan 4:26). The stump of Dagon is the opposite case: only the stump of the idol was left to him (1Sa 5:4).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines stump as the stub of a tree, plant or vegetable, that part of the stem which remains fixed in the earth when the stem is cut down.

expand to see more

STUMP, n. The stub of a tree, plant or vegetable; that part of the stem which remains fixed in the earth when the stem is cut down; as the stump of an oak.

2. The part of a limb of the body remaining after amputation.

Key Scripture

Dan 4:15 — "Nevertheless leave the stump of his roots in the earth, even with a band of iron and brass, in the tender grass of the field; and let it be wet with the dew of heaven, and let his portion be with the beasts in the grass of the earth:"

Dan 4:26 — "And whereas they commanded to leave the stump of the tree roots; thy kingdom shall be sure unto thee, after that thou shalt have known that the heavens do rule."

1Sa 5:4 — "And when they arose early on the morrow morning, behold, Dagon was fallen upon his face to the ground before the ark of the LORD; and the head of Dagon and both the palms of his hands were cut off upon the threshold; only the stump of Dagon was left to him. the"

Isa 6:13 — "But yet in it shall be a tenth, and it shall return, and shall be eaten: as a teil tree, and as an oak, whose substance is in them, when they cast their leaves: so the holy seed shall be the substance thereof."

Modern Corruption

Discipline is read as destruction, and Daniel's dream carefully preserves a stump because the humbling had an appointed end.

expand to see more

Daniel 4:15 contains the mercy inside the sentence: leave the stump of his roots in the earth. The tree is cut, the branches lopped, the leaves shaken off, and the beasts driven out — but the root is banded with iron and brass and kept. The interpretation makes the point explicit: thy kingdom shall be sure unto thee, after that thou shalt have known that the heavens do rule. The stump was the promise of restoration, banded so nothing could remove it.

Dagon's stump is the counter-case. The image fell before the ark twice; the second time the head and both palms were cut off upon the threshold, and only the stump of Dagon was left to him. A god that has to be set back in place by its worshippers, and finally cannot be, is what remains when the true God enters the room.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Aramaic iqqar (H6136), a stump or root-stock; Hebrew Dagon retains only its trunk in 1 Samuel 5:4; matstsebeth (H4678), a stump or pillar, in Isaiah 6:13.

expand to see more

Aramaic iqqar (H6136) — stump, root; Daniel 4:15, 23, 26.

Hebrew matstsebeth (H4678) — substance, stump; Isaiah 6:13, so the holy seed shall be the substance thereof.

Hebrew geza (H1503) — stem, stock; Isaiah 11:1, a rod out of the stem of Jesse.

Usage

"“Leave the stump of his roots in the earth” — mercy inside the sentence."

"“After that thou shalt have known that the heavens do rule” — the humbling had an end."

"“Only the stump of Dagon was left” — the idol that could not be propped up again."
